subject: forensic-medicine
title: Sexual Perversions: Sadism, Masochism and Fetishism

steps.title: Classification of sexual offences
steps.tx: Reddy sorts the field into **four groups of sexual offences**: natural offences such as rape, incest and adultery; unnatural offences such as sodomy, tribadism, bestiality and buccal coitus; sexual perversions such as sadism, masochism, necrophilia, fetishism, transvestism, exhibitionism, frotteurism and undinism; and sex linked offences such as stalking, voyeurism, sexual harassment, trafficking and indecent assault. The classification organises both this lesson and the next.
steps.say: Natural, unnatural, perversions and sex linked offences are the four shelves on which every sexual case is filed.

steps.title: Sadism, pleasure from suffering
steps.tx: **Sadism** is sexual arousal and gratification derived from inflicting pain, humiliation or suffering on another person. At its criminal extreme it drives lust murders, where mutilation of the victim, sometimes after death, accompanies the sexual act. Injuries in such cases are disproportionate, patterned and often genital or breast focused, which alerts the pathologist. The victim may be a stranger, and defence injuries may be absent where the attack was sudden or the victim was restrained.
steps.say: Sadism takes pleasure from the victim's suffering, and its extreme form explains mutilating lust murders at autopsy.

steps.tx: Arousal that depends on another person's pain can continue after that person is dead. In its forensic extreme, **sadism** leaves many wounds, often grouped on the genitals or the breasts, and more numerous than were needed to cause death. The pattern is what the pathologist records. A teaching model is used for the picture so that no real person is shown, and the face is covered. Defence injuries may be missing if the victim was tied or the first blow prevented a fight.
steps.say: Lust murder in sadism produces many patterned wounds, often genital or on the breast, beyond what killing required. The picture used in teaching is a model, with identity hidden. Defence wounds can be absent.

vis.alt: Teaching model of patterned mutilating injuries, with identifying features hidden.
vis.caption: A teaching model shows patterned injuries of the kind left when mutilation accompanies a sexual killing, with the face not shown. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Masochism, pleasure from being hurt
steps.tx: **Masochism** is the mirror pattern: sexual gratification from receiving pain, humiliation or restraint. Its forensic importance is accidental death during self applied or partner applied bondage and partial asphyxiation, where a solitary body with ligatures and no sign of struggle must not be misread as homicide. Scene details, padding to protect the neck, self rescue arrangements that failed and pornographic material together reconstruct the practice.
steps.say: Masochistic bondage deaths look staged like murder, until padding, self release gear and the scene explain an accident.

left.title: Accidental bondage death
points: Self rescue device present but failed

steps.title: Sadomasochism and consent boundaries
steps.tx: Combined sadomasochistic practice raises the legal question met in **consent to harm**: consent is no defence to the infliction of actual bodily harm in most legal systems, and a death during consensual rough practice is investigated as a potential homicide, not dismissed as an accident between partners. The examiner therefore documents every injury's age, pattern and severity and preserves ligatures and implements exactly as in any other neck compression death.
steps.say: Consent does not legalise bodily harm, so a death in rough practice is worked up like any other suspicious death.

rows: Consent is for court to judge

steps.title: Fetishism, arousal from objects
steps.tx: **Fetishism** is sexual arousal fixed on an inanimate object or a non genital body part, classically articles of clothing such as undergarments, shoes or handkerchiefs. It reaches the forensic clinic through thefts of such articles, sometimes in escalating series. By itself between consenting adults it harms no one; it becomes an offence when it drives stealing, trespass or exposure. History taking stays factual and free of ridicule, which keeps disclosure flowing.
steps.say: Fetishism fixes arousal on objects like clothing, and it enters forensic work through thefts rather than through violence.

nodes.label: Offence is the conduct, not desire

steps.tx: Sexual interest fixed on an object, classically underwear, shoes or a handkerchief, is **fetishism**. Between adults who agree, it harms nobody and it is not an offence. It comes to the police when the objects are stolen, sometimes as a series from a clothes line or a hostel. The items are sealed and labelled like any other exhibit. The history is taken without jokes. Ridicule is what stops the person describing how far the series goes.
steps.say: Fetishism fixes arousal on an object such as clothing or shoes. It is an offence only when it leads to theft, trespass or exposure. The articles are bagged as exhibits, and the history is taken without ridicule.

vis.alt: Shoes and items of clothing sealed in an evidence bag as fetish articles.
vis.caption: Items of clothing are sealed in an evidence bag as the articles of a fetish. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Transvestism and exhibitionism
steps.tx: **Transvestism** is arousal or emotional comfort from wearing clothes of the opposite sex, and it is not by itself an offence. **Exhibitionism** is exposure of the genitals to unsuspecting strangers for arousal, which is an offence and often the first sexual offence in a record. Distinguishing private cross dressing from public exposure matters because one is behaviour to note neutrally and the other is a chargeable act with a victim.
steps.say: Cross dressing privately is no offence, while exposing oneself to strangers is, and the record must separate the two.

steps.title: Frotteurism and undinism
steps.tx: **Frotteurism** is rubbing against a non consenting person, usually in a crowded place such as public transport, for sexual gratification. **Undinism** links arousal to water or urination. Both appear in examinations mainly through the behavioural history of an accused in repeated public complaints. A pattern of similar complaints at similar places and times is the evidence that matters, and it is assembled by investigators rather than by genital examination.
steps.say: Crowd rubbing and water linked arousal are diagnosed from repeated complaint patterns, not from any physical examination finding.

steps.title: Masturbation and the limits of law
steps.tx: Private **masturbation** is normal behaviour and no offence; it enters forensic practice only when performed publicly as indecent exposure or when a death during autoerotic practice is referred for autopsy. The examiner's language in reports stays clinical, because moralising language in a medicolegal document prejudices courts and shames families without adding a single fact. Age, privacy and consent remain the three tests that separate behaviour from offence.
steps.say: Privacy, adulthood and consent decide whether sexual behaviour concerns the law at all, and reports must stay clinical.

nodes.label: Offence only if an answer fails

steps.title: Examining an accused with a perversion history
steps.tx: In **assessment of sexual perversion cases**, the psychiatrist records the developmental history, onset, triggers, escalation, fantasies, previous complaints and response to treatment, and examines for mental illness that changes responsibility. Risk to identifiable groups, children above all, is stated plainly for the court. The physical examiner meanwhile treats any associated injury or disease. Neither examiner certifies that a perversion caused a specific act; that inference belongs to the trial.
steps.say: Record onset, triggers, escalation and risk honestly, treat the body, and leave causation of the act to the court.
